newsitem.title: UK: British government plans new strikes crackdown.
newsitem.headline: British government plans new strikes crackdown.

text.p: British Trade and Industry Secretary Ian Lang on Wednesday announced plans to allow people affected by strikes in monopoly public services to sue the trade union involved for damages.

"If in future, trade unions choose recklessly to overstep the limits of legitimate protest by exploiting monopoly power, they will face the consequences of their actions," he told the ruling Conservative Party's annual conference.
Lang said he would announce to parliament shortly a package of proposals that would bring the concept of "proportionality" into British industrial relations.
"If a strike's effect are disproportionately damaging to the public, then the trade union which organises the strike will risk losing its immunity and being sued for damages," he said.

He was accused in advance of "union bashing" by Alan Johnson, joint general secretary of the Communication Workers Union representing postal workers who have called several one-day strikes this year as part of a dispute over conditions.
Johnson told BBC radio that the government wanted to demonise workers in essential industries and the plans would effectively ban strikes in key public services.

But Lang denied the charge, saying: "We're not contemplating a ban on...strikes in certain services, what we're doing is looking at this from the point of view of the public and the effect this has on them."
Since taking power in 1979 the Conservatives have passed a series of laws severely clipping the powers of the once mighty trade unions.
But this summer saw a rash of strikes, with a series of disruptions on London's underground railway system among them.

Asked whether the current postal dispute could be the sort of action which would allow a company to sue for damage to its business, Lang said: "That would depend on the degree to which your business had suffered."
